newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris bids emotional farewell to Mastroianni.
newsitem.headline: Paris bids emotional farewell to Mastroianni.

text.p: - In death as in life, Marcello Mastroianni attracted women.

The women who adored him on the screen and in life crowded into an 18th century Paris church near the actor's home on the Left Bank on Friday -- along with far fewer men -- to bid an emotional farewell to Italy's quintessential Latin lover.
Mastroianni, who starred in some 160 films opposite some of cinema's most beautiful women, died of cancer in his Paris apartment on Thursday, aged 72.

His former lover, French actress Catherine Deneuve, their daughter Chiara Mastroianni, who is pregnant, and Anna-Maria Tato, his companion of the last 22 years, watched grimly from front-row pews as the coffin was carried down the aisle of the Saint Sulpice church.
Friends of the family said the church benediction -- no mass was performed -- was a compromise between Deneuve, a devout Catholic, and Tato who opposed it because the actor was not religious.
"He was a little afraid of these men who judge people," said a close family friend pointing to the priests. "Because he himself judged no one. They made him laugh."
Mastroianni's body was to be flown on Saturday to Rome, where he will lie in state at the Capitoline city hall until his civil funeral on Sunday.
"You make us think of a tender sun which we can admire without looking away, of the kindness of an artisan who leaves for work each morning with a smile," eulogised director Bertrand Blier.
"I don't know what it was you believed in, but you gave everyone else the desire to believe in it too. Even today," he said.

The score of "La Dolce Vita", Frederico Fellini's 1960 film which rocketed Mastroianni to fame, echoed eerily in the cavernous church as friends and family sprinkled the flower-laden coffin with holy water.
Chiara lovingly caressed her father's casket.
Besides several hundred fans, the guests included actors Gerard Depardieu, Michel Piccoli, Daniel Auteuil and Anouk Aimee, who played alongside him in "La Dolce Vita".
Italian director Marco Ferreri, who directed him in "Liza" and "La Grande Bouffe", was also present.

"I used to run into him in the neighbourhood," said Jean-Paul Marie, a neighbour. "I saw him often on mornings in Le Mandarin cafe where he had his coffee, and at the market on rue de Buci. He was very open and accessible."

"I adored that man -- his light, his humour, his tender smile," said Marie-Elena Fantasia, another fan. "It's a great loss. I saw (Ettore Scola's) "A Special Day' last night on television and it's a masterpiece," she added.
"A Special Day" was one of 12 films in which Mastroianni shared the screen with Italian actress Sophia Loren. The pair's on-screen chemistry always kept everyone guessing about real-life romance.

Outside, in a Felliniesque setting, hundreds of mourners gathered near a carousel and a glittering Christmas tree to watch as the pallbearers carried Mastroianni's coffin and set it gently in a hearse.
"Ciao Marcello", cried someone in the crowd.
